notesStmt.note: In a letter to Richard Maurice Bucke, dated November 4, 1888, Whitman notes that was in the process of working on a "short concluding note at end" for what he was calling "the big book." On November 10, Whitman wrote that he had "finished the little beginning & end Notes I spoke of for the big book and sent to the printer." This proof and its corrections, therefore, date from sometime after November 10, 1888, likely in mid-to-late November.
A corrected proof of "Note at end of Complete Poems and Prose," published in Complete Poems & Prose (1888–9).

body.p: As I conclude—and (to get typographical correctness,) after running my eyes diligently through the three big divisions of the preceding volume—the interrogative wonder-fancy rises in me whether (if it be not too arrogant to even state it,) the 33 years of my current time, 1855– ⹀/ hyphen 1888, with their aggregate of our New World doings and people, have not, indeed, created and formulated the foregoing leaves—forcing their utterance as the pages stand—coming actually from the direct urge and developments of those years, and not from any individual epic or lyrical attempts whatever, or from my pen or voice, or any body's special voice. Out of that supposition, the book might assume to be considere 'ˇd an autochthonic record and expression, freely render'd, of and out of these 30 to 35 years—of the soul and evolution of America—and of course, by reflection, ‸not ours only, but more or less of the common people of the world. . . . .‸

‸ Seems to me I may dare to claim a deep native tap-root for the book, too, in some sort. I came on the stage too late for personally knowning much of even the lingering Revolutionary worthies—the men of '76. Yet, as a little boy, I have been press'd tightly and lovingly to the breast of Lafayette, (Brooklyn, 1825,) and have talke 'ˇd with old Aaron Burr, and also with those who knew Washington and his surroundings, and with original Jeffersonians, and more than one very old soldier and sailor. And in my own day and maturity, my eyes have seen‸,/ and ears heard, Lincoln, Grant and Emerson, and my hands have been grasp'd by their hands. Though in a different field and range from most of theirs. ,/ I give the foregoing pages as perfectly legitimate, resultant, evolutionary and consistent with them. If these lines should ever reach some reader of a far off future age, let him take them as a missive sent from Abraham Lincoln's fateful age. . . . Repeating‸,/ parrot-like, what in the preceding divisions has been already said, and must serve as a great reason⹀why reason⹀why of this whole book—1st, That the main part about pronounc'd events and shows, (poems and persons also,) is the point of view from which they are view'd and estimated—and 2d, That I cannot let my momentous, stormy, peculiar Era
